text: Manipulator dynamics
A simple approach for ECE students
Single-link torque, energy methods, and coding activities
Craig Chapter 6 · Bridge to Chapter 7

Two meetings of about 50 minutes. Meeting 1 slides 1–9: physical torque, inertia, holding torque, payload and Coding Activity 1. Meeting 2 slides 10–20: energy derivation, forward dynamics, motion-time preview and Coding Activity 2. Four polls total, including an opening conceptual poll whose answer is explained on slide 5. Use two coding activities, about 8 and 12 minutes. Full 2R dynamics and release simulations are outside this compact deck.

Q1: A stationary arm
The arm is stationary and horizontal. Does the motor need to produce torque?
A.  Yes, to oppose gravity
B.  No, because acceleration is zero
C.  Only if the arm is moving
D.  Only if friction is present
Poll Everywhere · Q1

Poll Q1. Allow 1–2 minutes for individual calculation. Ask pairs to compare reasoning, then reveal the next slide. Correct answer: A. At rest the inertia and viscous-friction terms vanish, but gravity remains.

Inertia about the joint
A uniform rod has its center of mass at L/2.
The inertia about the center of mass is I_COM = mL?/12. About the joint, I_joint = mL?/3.
Greater inertia means greater torque for the same acceleration.

Q2: Holding at 30°

m = 2 kg, r꜀ = 0.3 m, g = 10 m/s².
At θ = 30°, θ̇ = 0, θ̈ = 0, what holding torque is required?
A.  0 N m
B.  3 N m
C.  6 N m
D.  12 N m
Poll Everywhere · Q2

Expected no-payload values 0,3,6,0 N m. With 0.5 kg payload 0,4.5,9,0. At 180° ideal gravity torque is zero but equilibrium is unstable. A horizontal tabletop arm with a vertical rotation axis has no gravity torque about that axis. Complete code is provided in Activity 1, students modify parameters.
Kinetic and potential energy
Kinetic energy measures motion.
Potential energy measures height relative to the lowest position.
The Lagrangian is ? = T ? V.
?h = r_c
The COM rises by r_c at 90?.

text: Treat angle and angular velocity as independent arguments for the partial derivatives. Hold angle fixed when differentiating with respect to velocity, and vice versa. I is constant. Forward dynamics
Inverse dynamics: known motion, calculate required torque.
Forward dynamics: known torque and state, calculate acceleration.
A simulation integrates acceleration to update velocity and angle.

Ask students to compare this with F=ma. Knowing torque does not determine angle immediately. The simulator uses RK4 and a small time step.

Q3: The released arm

I = 0.24 kg m², mgr꜀ = 6 N m.

B.  0 rad/s^2
D.  -25 rad/s^2
Poll Everywhere · Q3

Poll Q3. Allow 1–2 minutes for individual calculation. Ask pairs to compare reasoning, then reveal the next slide. Correct answer: A. Acceleration=(0-6*sin(30 deg))/0.24=-12.5 rad/s^2.

title: Q4: The same motion in half the time

text: Q4: The same motion in half the time

A cubic rest-to-rest motion takes 1 s instead of 2 s.
How do peak absolute velocity and acceleration change?
A.  Velocity x2, acceleration x2
B.  Velocity x2, acceleration x4
C.  Velocity x4, acceleration x2
D.  Both unchanged
Poll Everywhere · Q4

Poll Q4. Allow 1–2 minutes for individual calculation. Ask pairs to compare reasoning, then reveal the next slide. Correct answer: B. For unchanged normalized path, velocity scales as 1/T and acceleration as 1/T^2.
Source for energy formulation and dynamics structure: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/chapter-8-1-lagrangian-formulation-of-dynamics-part-1-of-2/ . All numerical examples and activities are original teaching examples.
Q4 answer: B
Velocity scales as 1/T_f, and acceleration as 1/T_f?.
Inertial torque quadruples. Total torque need not quadruple.

alt: Peak velocity doubles and peak acceleration quadruples

title: Coding activity 2: Motion time and torque

text: Coding activity 2: Motion time and torque
Run Activity 2. Compare 0° to 90° motions in 2 s and 1 s.
Report peak |θ̇|, |θ̈|, inertial torque and total torque.
Check a ±6 N m joint torque limit, including the final hold.
Repeat with a 0.5 kg tip payload. Explain whether slowing helps.
12 minutes · Submit plots, peak values, and a feasibility conclusion

12 minutes. Required torque is calculated for the desired path, not a simulated tracking controller. Check code peaks including endpoint values. Cubic acceleration is nonzero at endpoints. The final hold is a separate state. Sampled feasibility under an ideal symmetric limit is not hardware validation.
Source for energy formulation and dynamics structure: https://modernrobotics.northwestern.edu/nu-gm-book-resource/chapter-8-1-lagrangian-formulation-of-dynamics-part-1-of-2/ . All numerical examples and activities are original teaching examples.
Motion-time comparison

At the same s:

Gravity term is unchanged.
Friction term doubles.
Inertial term quadruples.

A payload needs 9 N m at the final hold.
No payload · Both motions reach the same final pose

These curves compare corresponding points on the same normalized path, not the same physical time. At s=1 the plotted torque includes deceleration. Immediately after the motion, stationary holding torque is 6 N m with no payload, or 9 N m with payload. Slowdown cannot eliminate the required static holding torque.
Next: Chapter 7 trajectory generation
Kinematics selects the joint configuration.
Trajectory generation specifies how that configuration changes over time.
Dynamics checks the torque required for that motion.
Feedback control helps the real robot follow the desired trajectory.

Next teach cubic coefficient derivation, joint-space interpolation and velocity/acceleration profiles. Revisit endpoint acceleration and quintic trajectories. Explain that joint-space interpolation does not generally create a straight Cartesian path.
